title: TopoDistill: Learning Topology for Causal Discovery
one_liner: A method that teaches a neural network to embed time-series data so neighborhoods match reality, making it easier to discover which variables cause which.
lead: To figure out which variable causes which in a time series (like temperature causing humidity), a classic method called convergent cross mapping reconstructs what the system looked like at past moments by stacking recent values into a high-dimensional point (an embedding: a list of numbers representing a moment). When data is noisy, this reconstruction gets muddled: points that should be neighbors become scattered, making it hard to tell causation apart from coincidence. TopoDistill teaches a small model to output numbers matching a stronger, fuller view of the system. Because the fuller view sees all variables at once, it preserves which points should be neighbors even when individual measurements are noisy, and TopoDistill transfers this knowledge to the smaller model. As a result, the small model's neighborhoods stay clean and causal links become visible even with noise.

problem.h2: Why reconstructing the past from fragments is hard
paras: When you want to discover causation in a time series (a stream of measurements over time), the standard trick is this: at each moment, stack the last N measurements into a list (a vector, which is just a list of numbers), treat that list as a single point in high-dimensional space, and use distances between points to infer causal links. The theory says this works — if you stack enough history, you can faithfully reconstruct the system's inner state. But real data is noisy. When noise garbles the reconstruction, nearby points scatter and distant ones cluster randomly. The consequence is brutal: the distance-based neighborhoods that the algorithm depends on become unreliable. You can't tell which variable nudges which because the signal is buried.

A beginner might try to filter the noise away, or use more history. But filtering removes detail and history just stacks more noise. The real problem is structural: a single noisy view of a multidimensional system can't faithfully capture which points should actually be neighbors.

callout.html: A noisy snapshot of a system's past states doesn't preserve which points should be neighbors, so distance-based causal discovery fails.

steps.text: Feed the full multivariate signal (all variables together) into a neural network, which learns which points should be neighbors.
Feed only time-lagged history (the classic stack) into a smaller neural network.
Measure which points are close in each embedding, then nudge the delay embedder so its neighborhood pattern matches the global embedder's.
Use the corrected delay embedder's output to discover causation, now with reliable neighbor information.
Points that are neighbors in the cleaned embedding yield true causal links, not noise correlations.

paras: TopoDistill changes how the delay embedder (the small network that stacks history) produces its output. Instead of passively stacking raw values with all their noise corruption, it actively learns a transformation that aligns its neighborhood structure to the cleaner, fuller view seen by the global embedder.

hidden.name: Neighborhood Alignment
paras: Neighborhood Alignment is a measure of how well the close points stay close between two different embeddings. Imagine two maps of the same city at different scales: the global embedder is a satellite view, the delay embedder is a street-level photo. Neighborhood Alignment asks: if two streets are neighbors in the satellite view, are they also neighbors in the street photo? If yes, the maps are well-aligned.

TopoDistill estimates this alignment by comparing the K-nearest neighbors (the K closest points) in each embedding. For each point, it finds its K neighbors in the global embedding and its K neighbors in the delay embedding, then measures how much they overlap. A high overlap means neighborhoods match; low overlap means they diverge. The paper uses this overlap score as the training signal: it nudges the delay embedder's weights until neighborhoods align.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger overlap in nearest neighbors; highlight marks alignment signal.

reads.html: The paper measures how many neighbors stay the same between the two embeddings. If most neighbors match, the embeddings agree on which points are close.

TopoDistill uses a neighborhood preservation loss: for each point, it penalizes when the K-nearest neighbors in the delay embedding diverge from the K-nearest neighbors in the global embedding, measured via a set-overlap or ranking correlation metric.

mechanism.h2: Why aligning neighborhoods fixes causation discovery
paras: The core mechanism: convergent cross mapping discovers causation by asking 'if I know the neighborhood of a point in variable A's history, can I predict the current state of variable B?' This only works if neighborhoods are honest. Noise breaks neighborhoods by scattering points that should be close. TopoDistill heals this by forcing the delay embedder to align its neighborhoods to the global embedder, which sees all variables at once and thus knows which points actually belong together. When neighborhoods are aligned, the algorithm can reliably say 'these two history-points are close because they represent truly similar system states, not random noise,' and therefore 'if A's history predicts B, then A causes B.' Without alignment, that claim is unreliable.

Why the global embedder is stronger: it trains on the full multivariate signal (all variables together), so it naturally learns a space where points that should be neighbors actually are neighbors in physical causality. The delay embedder, by contrast, only sees stacked history of individual variables and must guess which points belong together from fragments. By distilling the global embedder's knowledge into the delay embedder, the method transfers this understanding down, making the smaller model's neighborhoods match reality even when trained on partial information.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Imagine a time-series point x_5 (history at moment 5).
Global embedder says x_5's 3 nearest neighbors are: x_3, x_7, x_9 (confidence: they are close in the full system view).
Delay embedder initially says x_5's 3 nearest neighbors are: x_2, x_5, x_8 (a noisy guess).
Overlap: only x_5 appears in both lists, so overlap = 1 out of 3.
L_alignment for x_5 = penalty for (3 - 1) = 2 mismatches.
The delay embedder's weights are nudged to change x_5's embedding so that x_3, x_7, x_9 move closer.
After training, delay embedder says x_5's neighbors are: x_3, x_7, x_8 (now overlap = 2, penalty shrinks).
After many updates, delay embedder converges: x_5's neighbors match the global view almost perfectly.

math.note: The loss pushes the delay embedder to rotate and scale its output space so that neighborhoods match what the global embedder learned.

items.b: Global embedder overfits to a small dataset.
items.html: If the multivariate time series is short, the global embedder might memorize noise instead of learning which points should be neighbors. The distilled delay embedder then learns corrupted neighborhoods. Solution: regularize the global embedder or use a larger dataset.

items.b: Mismatch between global and delay embedder capacity.
items.html: If the delay embedder is too small, it cannot even learn to match the global embedder's neighborhoods, no matter the training signal. Neighborhoods stay misaligned. Solution: increase the delay embedder's hidden layer size.

items.b: Non-stationary time series (the rules change over time).
items.html: If the system's causal structure shifts over time (e.g., a valve opens halfway through), the global embedder learns a blended, confused view of which points should be neighbors. Distillation then teaches the wrong neighborhoods. Solution: split the data into stationary windows.

items.b: Done right: clean neighborhoods, honest causality.
items.html: When the embedders are well-matched and the data is stationary, neighborhoods are stable and cross-mapping reliably identifies causal links even under significant noise.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic three-variable time series where one variable (temperature) drives another (humidity) with a known lag, and a third (pressure) is independent noise. Apply convergent cross mapping with classic time-delay embedding versus TopoDistill. Measure: (1) True positive rate (how many true causal links are found), (2) False positive rate (how many spurious links are falsely detected). Plot these as noise level increases from 0 to 50 percent. The demo should show that classic time-delay embedding's true positive rate crashes as noise rises (because neighborhoods scatter), while TopoDistill maintains high true positive rate and low false positive rate across all noise levels.
demo.metric_eq: True causal link found = (confidence that temperature at time t-2 predicts humidity at time t) > threshold; False positive = (confidence that pressure predicts humidity) > threshold
demo.closing: The core insight: topology alignment makes neighborhoods so honest that they remain useful even when individual measurements are wildly noisy.
